request.user:
[2025 summer phd math-stat — problem 1]

Part III, Problem 1 (25 pts). Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. from a one-parameter exponential family $p(x \mid \theta) = h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta) T(x) - B(\theta)\}$, with $\eta(\theta)$ monotonically increasing and $\sum_i T(X_i)$ continuous.
(i) Construct the UMP test for $H_0 : \theta \le \theta_0$ vs $H_1 : \theta > \theta_0$.
(ii) Prove the test in (i) is uniformly most powerful.
(iii) Prove or disprove the existence of a UMP test for $H_0 : \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1 : \theta \ne \theta_0$.

response.text:
Let

\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i).
\]

The joint density is

\[
f_\theta(x_1,\dots,x_n)
=\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\exp\{\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta)\}.
\]

Assume throughout that \(0<\alpha<1\) is the desired level and that \(\theta_0\) is an interior point of the parameter space for the two-sided problem in part (iii). Also, interpret “\(\eta\) monotonically increasing” as strictly increasing, as is usual in an identifiable one-parameter exponential family.

---

## (i) UMP level-\(\alpha\) test for \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\)

For \(\theta_1>\theta_0\),

\[
\frac{f_{\theta_1}(X)}{f_{\theta_0}(X)}
=
\exp\left\{(\eta(\theta_1)-\eta(\theta_0))S_n-n(B(\theta_1)-B(\theta_0))\right\}.
\]

Since \(\eta(\theta_1)>\eta(\theta_0)\), the likelihood ratio is an increasing function of \(S_n\). Thus the family has a monotone likelihood ratio in \(S_n\).

Because \(S_n\) has a continuous distribution, choose \(c_\alpha\) such that

\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

Define the test

\[
\phi_\alpha(X_1,\dots,X_n)
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}.
\]

Equivalently, reject \(H_0\) when

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)>c_\alpha.
\]

This test has size \(\alpha\). Indeed, the monotone likelihood ratio property implies stochastic monotonicity of \(S_n\): if \(\theta_1>\theta_2\), then

\[
P_{\theta_1}(S_n>t)\ge P_{\theta_2}(S_n>t)
\]

for all \(t\). Hence

\[
\sup_{\theta\le \theta_0}P_\theta(S_n>c_\alpha)
=
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)
=
\alpha.
\]

Therefore the desired level-\(\alpha\) test is

\[
\boxed{\phi_\alpha=\mathbf 1\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)>c_\alpha\right\}},
\]

where \(c_\alpha\) satisfies \(P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha\).

---

## (ii) Proof that the test is uniformly most powerful

Let \(\psi\) be any other level-\(\alpha\) test for \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\). Then in particular

\[
E_{\theta_0}\psi\le \alpha.
\]

Fix any \(\theta_1>\theta_0\). We compare the power of \(\phi_\alpha\) and \(\psi\) at this fixed alternative.

Let

\[
\Lambda(X)=\frac{f_{\theta_1}(X)}{f_{\theta_0}(X)}
=
\exp\left\{(\eta(\theta_1)-\eta(\theta_0))S_n-n(B(\theta_1)-B(\theta_0))\right\}.
\]

Since \(\eta(\theta_1)>\eta(\theta_0)\), \(\Lambda(X)\) is increasing in \(S_n\). Thus for some \(k>0\),

\[
\phi_\alpha=\mathbf 1\{\Lambda>k\}.
\]

Moreover,

\[
E_{\theta_0}\phi_\alpha=\alpha\ge E_{\theta_0}\psi.
\]

Now

\[
E_{\theta_1}(\phi_\alpha-\psi)
=
E_{\theta_0}\left[\Lambda(\phi_\alpha-\psi)\right].
\]

Write

\[
E_{\theta_0}\left[\Lambda(\phi_\alpha-\psi)\right]
=
E_{\theta_0}\left[(\Lambda-k)(\phi_\alpha-\psi)\right]
+
kE_{\theta_0}(\phi_\alpha-\psi).
\]

The second term is nonnegative because

\[
E_{\theta_0}(\phi_\alpha-\psi)
=
\alpha-E_{\theta_0}\psi
\ge 0.
\]

The first term is also nonnegative pointwise. Indeed:

- On \(\{\Lambda>k\}\), \(\phi_\alpha=1\), so

  \[
  (\Lambda-k)(\phi_\alpha-\psi)
  =
  (\Lambda-k)(1-\psi)\ge 0.
  \]

- On \(\{\Lambda<k\}\), \(\phi_\alpha=0\), so

  \[
  (\Lambda-k)(\phi_\alpha-\psi)
  =
  (\Lambda-k)(-\psi)\ge 0.
  \]

- On \(\{\Lambda=k\}\), the product is zero; this set has probability zero because \(S_n\) is continuous.

Therefore

\[
E_{\theta_1}(\phi_\alpha-\psi)\ge 0.
\]

Hence

\[
E_{\theta_1}\phi_\alpha\ge E_{\theta_1}\psi.
\]

Since \(\theta_1>\theta_0\) was arbitrary, \(\phi_\alpha\) has power at least as large as any other level-\(\alpha\) test at every point in the alternative. Therefore \(\phi_\alpha\) is UMP.

Thus

\[
\boxed{\phi_\alpha=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}}
\]

is the UMP level-\(\alpha\) test of \(H_0:\theta\le\theta_0\) versus \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\).

This is precisely the Karlin–Rubin theorem for one-parameter exponential families with monotone likelihood ratio.

---

## (iii) Existence of a UMP test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta\ne \theta_0\)

In general, no nontrivial UMP level-\(\alpha\) test exists for the two-sided alternative.

Assume, for contradiction, that a UMP level-\(\alpha\) test \(\phi\) exists for

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0.
\]

Choose \(\theta_+>\theta_0\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the unique most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test of

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:\theta=\theta_+
\]

rejects for large values of \(S_n\). Hence it is

\[
\phi_+(X)=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_+\},
\]

where

\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_+)=\alpha.
\]

If \(\phi\) were UMP for the two-sided alternative, then in particular it would have to be most powerful against the simple alternative \(\theta_+\). By uniqueness in the Neyman–Pearson lemma, this forces

\[
\phi=\phi_+
\qquad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Now choose \(\theta_-<\theta_0\). Then

\[
\frac{f_{\theta_-}(X)}{f_{\theta_0}(X)}
=
\exp\left\{(\eta(\theta_-)-\eta(\theta_0))S_n-n(B(\theta_-)-B(\theta_0))\right\}.
\]

Since \(\eta(\theta_-)<\eta(\theta_0)\), this likelihood ratio is decreasing in \(S_n\). Therefore the Neyman–Pearson most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test of

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:\theta=\theta_-
\]

rejects for small values of \(S_n\). Thus it is

\[
\phi_-(X)=\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_-\},
\]

where

\[
P_{\theta_0}(S_n<c_-)=\alpha.
\]

Again, if \(\phi\) were UMP for the two-sided alternative, it would have to be most powerful against \(\theta_-\). By uniqueness of the Neyman–Pearson test,

\[
\phi=\phi_-
\qquad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Thus we would need

\[
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_+\}
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_-\}
\qquad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

But this is impossible for \(0<\alpha<1\). The set \(\{S_n>c_+\}\) is an upper tail of probability \(\alpha\), while \(\{S_n<c_-\}\) is a lower tail of probability \(\alpha\). Since \(S_n\) is continuous and nondegenerate, these two rejection regions cannot coincide up to a null set.

Therefore no nontrivial UMP test exists for the two-sided alternative.

Hence

\[
\boxed{\text{There is no UMP level-}\alpha\text{ test for }H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\text{ vs. }H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0,\ 0<\alpha<1.}
\]

This is why, in two-sided one-parameter exponential-family testing problems, one usually considers likelihood ratio tests or UMP unbiased tests rather than UMP tests.
